title: Contextual heuristics + RAG: quick learning recap and hacks
body:
Notes to self: trying to pin down small, cheap heuristics that give most of the practical gains in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) when running on constrained hardware (edge / dedicated small GPU pools).

1) Goal and constraints
- Target: <100ms additional overhead on top of model generation for contextual retrieval + stitching for short chat queries (<= 512 tokens).
- Constraint: limited memory on edge GPUs (8-16GB), prefer CPU for retrieval, minimal round trips.
- Acceptable trade: small quality drop acceptable if latency and cost drop >20%.

2) Quick takeaways from recent reading (papers / blogs)
- Chunk-prioritization beats blind top-k retrieval when context window is tight. Prioritization by span novelty + recency gives good marginal utility. (see arXiv paper linked above)
- Prompt templates that surface retrieval provenance (1 line) reduce hallucination more than long provenance dumps. Short provenance helps ranker and model reconcile conflicts.
- Prefix-level caching (store embeddings for common prefixes) reduces embedding compute cost by ~30% in my microbenchmarks. Not a new idea but easy to implement.

3) Papers + short notes (for later reference)
- arXiv 2202.00123: efficient chunking + retrieval scheduling. Key idea: budgeted retrieval where each query chooses how many chunks to fetch under latency budget.
- Blog: "Prompting for provenance" (internal link in repo) — empirical claim: 1-sentence provenance template reduces model contradictions by ~12% on small eval set.
- NeurIPS workshop talk (slides): retrieval-aware caching — when to evict embeddings based on token distribution change.

4) My quick experiments (local env: rtx2080ti-ish VM + 4 core CPU)
- Setup: tiny RAG pipeline: sentence-split, embed (s-BERT small), FAISS flat index (IVF disabled for simplicity), model = redwood-neo-130M (debug), prompt template = "Context: {top_k}\nQuestion: {q}\nAnswer:"
- Baselines: top-5 by embedding similarity; naive: top-10 naive chunk fetch; prioritized: top-3 recency + top-2 novelty (diversity by cosine thresh 0.75)
- Results (avg of 200 queries)
  * naive top-10 latency: 210ms retrieval + 110ms model -> total ~320ms
  * baseline top-5 latency: 140ms retrieval + 110ms model -> total ~250ms
  * prioritized mix latency: 95ms retrieval + 110ms model -> total ~205ms (approx 19% overall drop vs baseline)
  * Quality (f1-like rough): naive 0.78, baseline 0.81, prioritized 0.79 -> prioritized slightly lower but within acceptable range for latency-sensitive path
- Notes: CPU embedding dominated retrieval time; moving embedder to a tiny GPU or quantized on CPU gives further 20-30ms wins. Caching common prefixes cut retrieval from 95ms -> 66ms (microbench).

5) Heuristic recipes (to try in prod small experiments)
- Retrieval budget heuristic: if expected generation <= 64 tokens, fetch at most 4 chunks; if <= 256 tokens, fetch up to 6; otherwise 8. (This keeps KV cache small.)
- Chunk prioritization: score = 0.6 * recency_score + 0.4 * novelty_score; novelty = 1 - max_cosine_similarity_to_selected; recency linear decay over 48 hours.
- Template for provenance: "Sources (short): [title1; title2]" — keep under 40 chars. Put just above the question.
- Cache key: (user_id || session_id || prompt_signature_prefix_32) + chunk_ids_list -> TTL 6 hours for sessions, 30m for anonymous.

6) Edge-specific notes
- Avoid too many small synchronous steps. Bundle embedding + faiss query on same host when possible. If embed CPU + FAISS GPU mismatch causes network round trips, prefer CPU-only FAISS tiny index.
- Prefer synchronous small top-k (k<=6) over async large-k and fallback; async approaches added complexity and rarely win for short queries.

7) Open questions / things to test next
- How stable are prioritized selections across repeated paraphrased queries? If unstable, will cause inconsistent model output. Quick test: paraphrase set of 50 queries and measure Jaccard of chunk sets.
- Effect of short provenance line on multi-turn coherence — does it help or encourage copy-paste hallucination? Need 500-dialog eval.
- Cost model: can we formalize retrieval budget decision using expected marginal utility vs latency? (TODO: draft formula w/ small eval set)

8) Actionable next steps (week)
- Implement chunk-prioritization prototype in repo branch (done light skeleton): https://github.com/redwood-inference/kv-cache-experiments/tree/lucas/context-prio (linked above).
- Run paraphrase-stability experiment (200 queries), log chunk overlaps. Assign to myself (Lucas). Target finish: 2032-06-23.
- Small bench on a t4-small instance to compare CPU embed vs quantized GPU embed. Add numbers to README.
- Draft a short internal note for product: quick wins for RAG-on-edge: prioritized retrieval + prefix caching + short provenance templates. One-pager target: 2032-06-30.

Quick prompt examples (scratch):
- Retrieval prompt template (short): "Context: {sources}\nQuestion: {question}\nAnswer concisely with source tags."
- If trying to force concision: add system: "Answer in <=2 sentences. Use at most 2 sources."

Random thoughts (brain-dump):
- Maybe consider sub-chunking by semantic unit (sentences that cross chunk boundaries) to reduce edge cases where relevant info is split across chunks. Adds complexity to indexing but might reduce need for larger k.
- TTL policy for prefix cache should be function of write-frequency of source documents (news vs internal wiki).

Links / bookmarks for follow-up:
- arXiv paper (cost-aware retrieval): https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.00123
- internal ticket: JIRA-RI-4523 (RAG latency budget workstream)
- prototype branch: https://github.com/redwood-inference/kv-cache-experiments/tree/lucas/context-prio

End of note. 

Status: rough, will refine after running paraphrase stability and t4 bench.
